::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.research_questions:
The significant public health burden of anorexia nervosa (AN) and the rising hospitalization rates since the COVID-19 pandemic underscore the urgent need for effective and accessible ED interventions in pediatric medical settings. Family Based Treatment (FBT) is the recommended first-line treatment for youth with AN, in which parents are put in charge of choosing, providing, and supervising all meals and snacks until the patient is weight restored, at which point independence is then gradually transitioned back to the patient. Unfortunately, families face significant challenges with the implementation of FBT. One contributing factor is the high levels of family conflict due to patient distress about eating and weight gain. For example, when presented with food or when weight increases, patients may engage in behaviors such as negotiating, yelling, crying, throwing food, or becoming aggressive. In turn, parents experience various emotional and behavioral reactions to their child’s distress, including parental accommodation behaviors (e.g., ending the meal, offering a lower calorie food, reducing the amount of food, etc.), which negatively impacts their child’s illness course and treatment outcomes. Distress tolerance, or the capacity to endure negative psychological states, is often linked to lower levels of accommodation behaviors. In other words, caregivers who are more inclined to avoid distressing situations may engage in more accommodation, leading to greater difficulties consistently implementing changes to promote weight gain for a child with AN, though research in this area remains limited. Lack of access to FBT providers, especially those accepting Medicaid insurance, exacerbates the challenges families face in implementing treatment. In the Chicago area, only one Medicaid plan is in-network with higher levels of ED care programs (e.g., partial hospitalization and intensive outpatient programs) and most FBT therapists operate on a self-pay or out-of-network basis, rendering expedient continuation of care inaccessible for many families. In Illinois, 40.90% of Medicaid-enrolled children identify as Hispanic, underscoring the disproportionate impact of limited treatment options on minoritized families. Providing a single-session intervention (SSI), Empower-ED, as an adjunctive treatment for caregivers of youth with AN admitted to Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children’s Hospital of Chicago (LCH) for medical stabilization before transitioning to outpatient FBT has the potential to optimize care during the hospitalization and support a smooth transition between care settings.  

While this study is exploratory, we aim to gather preliminary evidence regarding the feasibility, acceptability, and potential utility of Empower-ED. Specifically, we seek to explore the following research questions: 
- Feasibility: What is the feasibility of implementing Empower-ED with caregivers of youth with AN during inpatient medical treatment? 
- Acceptability: How acceptable is the intervention to caregivers in terms of its content and delivery? 
- Intervention Utility: What within-group changes in outcomes do people who completed the intervention report?  
- Equity: Is Empower-ED equally feasible and acceptable for both English- and Spanish-speaking caregivers as well as private and publicly insured families?
table.design_dependent_variables:
OUTCOMES 
- Accommodation and Enabling Scale for Eating Disorders: Asks respondents to rate 33 items assessing whether and how caregivers are drawn into accommodating and enabling their loved one’s ED. Per IRB requirements, the item “Does your loved one engage any family member in repeated conversations about self-harm?” was omitted. Assessed at pre-intervention and 3-month follow-up. 
- Distress Tolerance Scale: Asks respondents to rate 16 items assessing perceived capacity to tolerate distress. Assessed at pre-intervention, 1-2 week follow-up, and 3-month follow-up. 
- Current Distress Items: Asks respondents to rate 2 items assessing perceived ability to manage and tolerate their child’s distress related to their ED and associated treatment. The items are “Right now, I feel very prepared to help my child manage distress related to their eating disorder” and “Right now, I feel very prepared to tolerate my child's distress related to eating disorder treatment.” Assessed pre-intervention, immediately post-intervention, 1-2 week follow-up, and 3-month follow-up. 
- Parents versus Anorexia scale: Asks respondents to rate 7 items assessing perceived self-efficacy in taking charge over their child’s ED. Assessed at pre-intervention, immediately post-intervention, 1-2 week follow-up, and 3-month follow-up. 
- Parent Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire: Asks respondents to report on ED symptoms and behaviors that they have observed in their child in the previous 28 days. The measure’s content and scoring mirrors the EDE-Q. Assessed at pre-intervention and 3-month follow-up. 
- Program Feedback Scale: Asks respondents to rate 7 statements assessing intervention acceptability and feasibility. Also includes open-ended items that invite respondents to share what they liked and/or would change about the intervention. Assessed immediately post-intervention. 
- Patient records: Patient variables such as readmission rates, weight changes, FBT attrition, and session attendance will be collected from medical chart review. Assessed over the course of 3-months post-intervention. 

DEMOGRAPHICS 
- Race/Ethnicity 
- Primary Language 
- Socioeconomic Status (i.e., income bracket) 
- Insurance Type 
- Prior Treatment Access 

PATTERNS OF USE  
- Number of individuals who began the SSI, regardless of completion 
- Number of individuals who complete the SSI in full 
- Time spent on the SSI (in minutes/seconds) 
- Number of individuals who complete the Program Feedback Scale  
- Number of individuals who complete of all pre-intervention and post-intervention questionnaires 
- Number of individuals who complete the optional focus group questions 
- Number of individuals who complete the follow-up questionnaires
table.study_design_overview: This is a non-randomized pilot study, meaning that all caregivers will receive the intervention. Project Empower-Eating Disorders (Empower-ED) is a web-based SSI that provides caregivers psychoeducation on EDs and treatment, guidance on identifying avoidance patterns, support for creating personalized action plans to reduce accommodation behaviors, normalization of caregiver distress responses, and an anxiety management vignette. The goal is to enhance caregiver distress tolerance during meals, reduce accommodation behaviors, and ultimately improve treatment outcomes and access. Empower-ED is an adaptation of a self-guided, web-based SSI designed to reduce parental accommodation of child anxiety, which has already shown short-term efficacy and acceptability (Sung et al., 2021).
table.statistical_tests:
We will compute descriptive statistics for all “Patterns of Use” variables specified above. We will report demographic factors, as percentages of the total sample, for all demographic indicators collected. We will also report mean scores and standard deviations for all outcome measures.   

Intervention feasibility will be assessed by SSI completion rates. Mean Program Feedback Scale scores will be evaluated, with scores above 3 (on a 5-point scale) indicating acceptability.  

We will examine within-group changes in caregivers' perceived ability to manage their child's AN recovery-related distress and self-efficacy (measured by the Parent Vs. Anorexia Scale, Distress Tolerance Scale, and Current Distress Items), among caregivers who completed the SSI, at the following timepoints: pre-SSI, immediately post-SSI, 1–2 weeks follow-up, and 3 months follow-up. Paired t-tests, Cohen’s dz, and 95% confidence intervals will be reported to evaluate changes across these timepoints. 

At the 3-month follow-up, we will also examine within-group changes in caregiver-reported accommodation behaviors (measured by the Accommodation and Enabling Scale for Eating Disorders) and caregiver ratings of their child's symptom severity (measured by the Parent Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire), among caregivers who completed the SSI, from baseline to 3 months. Paired t-tests, Cohen’s dz, and 95% confidence intervals will be reported to evaluate changes across these timepoints.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Exclusion Criteria: 
1) Parents/Caregivers are not the legal guardians of the patient. 
2) The patient is admitted for a condition other than medical stabilization related to anorexia nervosa. 
3) The patient is under 7 years old or over 24 years old. For patients over 18, exclusion applies if there is no identified caregiver responsible for the patient’s treatment who is willing or able to participate in the study. 
4) Parents/Caregivers are unable to read and understand either English or Spanish. 
5) The patient does not plan to receive follow-up medical care with Lurie Children's Eating Disorder program after discharge.
table.sample_size: Our target sample size is 25 caregivers of unique patients with AN.
table.additional_comments:
Caregivers will be asked if they are interested in participating in an optional online focus group in which they will respond to open-ended feedback questions with written responses. 

Pending the sample size of those who complete this optional component, an exploratory qualitative analysis of responses will be conducted. Pending data availability from electronic medical records, descriptive statistics will be used to report patient readmission rates, weight changes, FBT attrition in care-as-usual outpatient, and care-as-usual session attendance at 1-2 weeks and 3 months post-intervention. 

Pending sample characteristics (i.e., distribution of participants with Medicaid vs private insurance), subgroup analyses will explore differences in outcomes (all outcome measures collected, feasibility, acceptability, and clinical variables such as follow-up adherence, weight gain, re-admissions) by insurance type (Medicaid vs. private). Pending sample characteristics (i.e., distribution of caregivers with English vs Spanish as their preferred language), we will conduct the same comparisons as above. Non-randomized program evaluation

text.text: The authors used Claude to assist in preparing code for the study analyses.

All AI-assisted code and resulting outputs were reviewed, verified, and approved by the study authors, who take full responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of the analyses and reported results.
No specific efforts were taken to involve persons with lived experience in the study design or execution, or in the preparation of this manuscript.
-Project EMPOWER-ED is a brief web-based caregiver SSI targeting accommodation of eating disorder behaviors.
-Twenty-five caregivers of child/adolescents admitted for inpatient medical stabilization treatment of anorexia nervosa completed Project EMPOWER-ED.
-Feasibility of Project EMPOWER-ED was high, and caregivers found the intervention to be highly acceptable.
-Results suggested that Project EMPOWER-ED had high uptake and completion rates, and promising preliminary changes on measures of perceived preparedness and distress tolerance.
Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a serious eating disorder that can become chronic and potentially life-threatening.

Hospitalizations for AN among American youth have increased, making pediatric medical settings an increasingly important part of the treatment continuum 1,2. When youth with AN are hospitalized, the immediate priority is their nutritional rehabilitation and medical stabilization-however, hospitalization also represents an important opportunity to support caregivers (including parents, guardians, and other custodial adults) as they navigate their child's next stages of treatment.
text.formatted: Hospitalizations for AN among American youth have increased, making pediatric medical settings an increasingly important part of the treatment continuum <ref type="bibr">1,2.</ref> When youth with AN are hospitalized, the immediate priority is their nutritional rehabilitation and medical stabilization-however, hospitalization also represents an important opportunity to support caregivers (including parents, guardians, and other custodial adults) as they navigate their child's next stages of treatment.

text.text: Though caregivers play a crucial role in the treatment of children and adolescents with AN, many feel uncertain about how to respond effectively to the illness and doubt their ability to support their child's recovery. 3, 4 In particular, caregivers report difficulties during care transitions from higher to lower levels of care. 5 Though caregivers play a central role in supporting ongoing nutritional rehabilitation and recovery, structured approaches to preparing caregivers for these responsibilities are not routinely integrated into inpatient medical care 6, 7.
text.formatted: Though caregivers play a crucial role in the treatment of children and adolescents with AN, many feel uncertain about how to respond effectively to the illness and doubt their ability to support their child's recovery. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> In particular, caregivers report difficulties during care transitions from higher to lower levels of care. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> Though caregivers play a central role in supporting ongoing nutritional rehabilitation and recovery, structured approaches to preparing caregivers for these responsibilities are not routinely integrated into inpatient medical care <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref>.

text.text: Transitions in care often require caregivers to take the lead in responding to their child's eating disorder behaviors and maintaining expectations for meals and exercise.

Caregivers of young people with AN frequently report high levels of fear, emotional distress, and burden, which may make it more difficult to respond confidently and consistently to their child's eating disorder-driven behaviors and distress 8, 9 .
text.formatted: Caregivers of young people with AN frequently report high levels of fear, emotional distress, and burden, which may make it more difficult to respond confidently and consistently to their child's eating disorder-driven behaviors and distress <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: In an understandable effort to reduce their child's symptoms, manage their own fear, or avoid escalating conflict, caregivers may accommodate the eating disorder by modifying meals, permitting avoidance of feared foods, participating in eating disorder rituals, or reorganizing family routines around symptoms 10 .
text.formatted: In an understandable effort to reduce their child's symptoms, manage their own fear, or avoid escalating conflict, caregivers may accommodate the eating disorder by modifying meals, permitting avoidance of feared foods, participating in eating disorder rituals, or reorganizing family routines around symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: Although accommodation may reduce distress in the short term, it may also reinforce avoidance and make it more difficult to maintain recovery-oriented behaviors 11.
text.formatted: Although accommodation may reduce distress in the short term, it may also reinforce avoidance and make it more difficult to maintain recovery-oriented behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref>.

text.text: Caregiver self-efficacy, defined as caregivers' confidence in their ability to support their child's recovery, may be particularly important in navigating these challenges 12 .
text.formatted: Caregiver self-efficacy, defined as caregivers' confidence in their ability to support their child's recovery, may be particularly important in navigating these challenges <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Greater caregiver self-efficacy has been associated with improved weight-related outcomes in treatment, and as such, is a core target for the majority of multiple evidence-based child and adolescent outpatient eating disorder interventions [13] [14] [15] [16] .
text.formatted: Greater caregiver self-efficacy has been associated with improved weight-related outcomes in treatment, and as such, is a core target for the majority of multiple evidence-based child and adolescent outpatient eating disorder interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> .

text.text: One study found that caregiver self-efficacy may remain relatively unchanged during brief medical admissions, highlighting hospitalization as a potential opportunity to strengthen caregivers' confidence before they transition to supporting continued recovery at home 17.
text.formatted: One study found that caregiver self-efficacy may remain relatively unchanged during brief medical admissions, highlighting hospitalization as a potential opportunity to strengthen caregivers' confidence before they transition to supporting continued recovery at home <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref>.

text.text: Single-session interventions (SSIs) offer a promising approach to addressing this gap.
SSIs are structured interventions designed to provide a meaningful therapeutic experience within a single encounter, regardless of what supports are accessed before or after 18, 19 .
text.formatted: SSIs are structured interventions designed to provide a meaningful therapeutic experience within a single encounter, regardless of what supports are accessed before or after <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: Brief, selfguided, web-based SSIs may be particularly well suited for delivery during medical hospitalization because of their relative low burden, which is crucial given the numerous competing demands during a child's medical crisis.
One such digital SSI is Project EMPOWER (available at https://www.leafbyleaf.org/empower), an approximately 30-minute, web-based, self-administered SSI for caregivers of youth with anxiety symptoms.
text.formatted: One such digital SSI is Project EMPOWER (available at <ref type="url" target="https://www.leafbyleaf.org/empower">www.leafbyleaf.org/empower</ref>), an approximately 30-minute, web-based, self-administered SSI for caregivers of youth with anxiety symptoms.

text.text: The intervention teaches parents to recognize accommodating behaviors in their own daily routines, understand how those behaviors can inadvertently sustain their child's anxious avoidance, and guides them to build a personalized plan for reducing these behaviors.
Project EMPOWER has been evaluated in three randomized trials, demonstrating high acceptability, feasibility, and effectiveness among caregivers of diverse socioeconomic status 20- 22 .
text.formatted: Project EMPOWER has been evaluated in three randomized trials, demonstrating high acceptability, feasibility, and effectiveness among caregivers of diverse socioeconomic status <ref type="bibr">20- 22</ref> .

text.text: Project EMPOWER reduced accommodating behaviors (ds = 0.49-0.61) across three trials where this outcome was measured at follow-up, relative to an informational control.

Although Project EMPOWER was designed for caregivers of children struggling with anxiety, the process it targets-caregiver accommodation of their child's disorder-driven behaviors-appears across many forms of psychopathology 11 .
text.formatted: Although Project EMPOWER was designed for caregivers of children struggling with anxiety, the process it targets-caregiver accommodation of their child's disorder-driven behaviors-appears across many forms of psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: Accommodation is especially salient in AN, which can look like buying only low-calorie foods, going along with rigid mealtime rituals, or repeatedly offering reassurance 10 .
text.formatted: Accommodation is especially salient in AN, which can look like buying only low-calorie foods, going along with rigid mealtime rituals, or repeatedly offering reassurance <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: Reaching caregivers directly through a single-session, self-administered format could extend support to many caregivers around eliminating accommodation.
As such, an adaptation of Project EMPOWER was developed for caregivers of young patients with AN, called Project EMPOWER-ED.
The purpose of this paper is to describe the development, feasibility, and acceptability of Project EMPOWER-ED for a sample of caregivers of patients hospitalized for AN.
Study procedures were approved by the Lurie Children's Hospital Institutional Review Board.
Informed consent was obtained for all enrolled families.
The data collection and analytic plan was pre-registered on Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/4amf7) and all deviations to the pre-registration are outlined in Supplement 1.
text.formatted: The data collection and analytic plan was pre-registered on Open Science Framework (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/4amf7">https://osf.io/4amf7</ref>) and all deviations to the pre-registration are outlined in Supplement 1.

text.text: Data collection occurred between January 13, 2025 and May 30, 2025.
Participants were recruited at a large, urban pediatric hospital in the Midwest.
The hospital sees patients ages 7 to 25 years old in need of medical stabilization due to AN, with approximately half of AN-related admissions are covered by Medicaid.

Eligible participants were the legal guardians of patients who met the following criteria: (1) patient's primary admission diagnosis was AN, and (2) caregiver ability to read and write in English or Spanish.
All study materials were available in both English and Spanish, and participants could decide which language they preferred.
Prior to discharge, caregivers completed a baseline survey and the SSI on either a hospital-provided iPad or via a secure online link.
The baseline survey included pre-intervention questionnaires, the SSI, and post-intervention questionnaires.
Taken together, the baseline survey and SSI took about an hour to complete.
Participants who completed this portion received a $25 gift card.

Demographics: At pre-intervention, caregivers completed a demographic questionnaire assessing caregiver and patient race/ethnicity, caregiver gender identity, caregiver's relationship to the patient, caregiver's marital status and caretaking responsibilities, caregiver language, caregiver education, caregiver income, suspected family history of an eating disorder, patient's eating disorder treatment history, and patient's age.

Additional demographic information was obtained electronic medical record review including patient's healthcare coverage, patient's cooccurring psychiatric conditions, patient's length of medical stabilization admission, and patient's body mass index (BMI) at admission.

Feasibility: Feasibility was assessed through intervention enrollment and completion metrics, including the proportion of eligible caregivers who initiated and completed the intervention, completed pre-post assessments, and completed the qualitative feedback questions.
Intervention duration was also recorded.

Acceptability: Acceptability was assessed immediately post-intervention using the 7-item Program Feedback Scale (PFS) designed to evaluate acceptability brief, web-based, self-guided interventions 27 .
text.formatted: Acceptability: Acceptability was assessed immediately post-intervention using the 7-item Program Feedback Scale (PFS) designed to evaluate acceptability brief, web-based, self-guided interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> .

text.text: The PFS was originally used with adolescents and was therefore modified for the current study to target caregivers' perceptions (e.g., replaced the word "kids" with "caregivers" in the item "I think the program would be helpful to other caregivers"), aligning with other research involving caregivers 20 .
text.formatted: The PFS was originally used with adolescents and was therefore modified for the current study to target caregivers' perceptions (e.g., replaced the word "kids" with "caregivers" in the item "I think the program would be helpful to other caregivers"), aligning with other research involving caregivers <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> .

text.text: Items evaluated caregiver enjoyment of the program, understanding of the material, ease of use, engagement during the program, perceived helpfulness for other caregivers, willingness to recommend the program to others, and agreement with the intervention's message.
Responses were rated on a 5-point Likert scale, with higher scores indicating greater acceptability.
An overall acceptability score was calculated by averaging responses across items, with a mean overall score ≥3 indicating that the intervention is acceptable.
Qualitative Feedback: A total of nine open-ended questions were displayed to participants at post-intervention.

Participants could respond to these questions about intervention aspects they found helpful, intervention aspects they would change, their perception of how engaging with the intervention may impact their responses to their child's eating disorder behavior, their opinion about optimal timing of the intervention (i.e., when during their child's treatment it would be most helpful), and their opinion about the digital self-guided format.
Caregiver Preparedness: Two investigator-developed items assessed caregiver preparedness at pre-intervention and immediately post-interventions.
Caregivers rated their preparedness to (1) help their child manage eating disorder-related distress and (2) tolerate their child's distress related to eating disorder treatment.
Responses were provided on a 5-point Likert scale, with higher scores indicating greater preparedness.

Project EMPOWER-ED was developed through an iterative, stakeholder-engaged adaptation process involving Project EMPOWER developers and three psychologists with expertise in pediatric eating disorder treatment.
These stakeholders reviewed the original intervention and provided detailed feedback regarding its relevance and application to eating disorder care.
The intervention developers then elicited additional input through collaborative discussion and iterative content revision, followed by further review and refinement by the clinical-research team.

This process preserved the original intervention's focus on avoidance, accommodation, emotion-focused validation, and personalized action planning while adapting these principles to the specific demands of supporting a loved one's eating disorder recovery.

The version of Project EMPOWER-ED evaluated in this pilot study included: (1) psychoeducation about eating disorders, eating disorder-driven avoidance, and caregiver accommodation; (2) strategies for recognizing and responding to eating disorder-driven avoidance while validating distress and maintaining nutritional expectations; (3) interactive vignette to reinforce these concepts in which caregivers identified avoidance, accommodation, and caregiver vulnerabilities; (4) development of a personalized action plan to reduce accommodation and support consistent caregiver responses; and (5) links to optional resources addressing caregiver distress, social support, food insecurity, and access to specialized care.
Descriptive Statistics: We calculated demographic factors, as percentages of the total sample, for all applicable demographic indicators collected.

We calculated means and standard deviations for patient' age, patients' length of medical stabilization admission, patients' BMI at admission, and caregivers' level of distress tolerance at baseline to further characterize the sample.

To assess feasibility, we calculated out of the total number of invited potential participants, the proportion of participants who (1) began the SSI, (2) completed the SSI, (3) completed the Program Feedback Scale, (4) completed all pre-intervention and postintervention questionnaires, and ( 5) completed the open-ended focus group questions.
text.formatted: To assess feasibility, we calculated out of the total number of invited potential participants, the proportion of participants who (1) began the SSI, (2) completed the SSI, (3) completed the Program Feedback Scale, (4) completed all pre-intervention and postintervention questionnaires, and ( <ref type="formula">5</ref>) completed the open-ended focus group questions.

text.text: An additional pattern of intervention use, the mean and standard deviation of time spent completing the SSI, was derived using the interquartile range (IQR) method to exclude page-level outliers more than 1.5 times the IQR below the first quartile or above the third quartile.
To assess intervention acceptability, we calculated the means and standard deviations for the PFS sum score as well as for the individual PFS items.
We plotted the PFS sum score of each participant to visualize the distribution of acceptability ratings.

These explorations of acceptability were conducted for the overall sample as well as for subgroups stratified by language (English and Spanish), Insurance Coverage (Public Insurance and Private Insurance), and Education Level as dichotomized during analysis (More Education defined as caregivers who reported obtaining a college degree or above and Less Education defined as caregivers who reported educational attainment less than completing college).

While the small sample size and pilot nature of this study precludes claims about intervention effectiveness, we descriptively evaluated pre-to-post change in caregiver preparedness to (1) help their child manage eating disorder-related distress and (2) tolerate their child's distress related to eating disorder treatment.
We calculated the mean and standard deviation for each item at pre-intervention and post-intervention and derived the difference scores.
Qualitative Analysis: Two coders conducted inducted content analysis on responses to nine post-SSI open-ended feedback questions 28 .
text.formatted: Qualitative Analysis: Two coders conducted inducted content analysis on responses to nine post-SSI open-ended feedback questions <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> .

text.text: Individually, coders familiarized themselves with the data and generated initial codebooks.
The coders then met to compare codebooks and generate a combined codebook.
The coders separately used the combined codebook to code each response.
Meetings were held for the coders to resolve discrepancies and refine the definitions included in the codebook.
This process was repeated and the combined codebook updated until all responses were coded with consensus.

The caregivers enrolled in the study were primarily biological mothers (80.00%) and endorsed diverse racial and ethnic identities, with 48.00% identifying as white non-Hispanic, 44.00% identifying as Hispanic/Latinx/Latine, and 8.00% identifying as Asian.
One-fifth (n=5) of the caregivers selected to use the Spanish-language version of the intervention, indicating Spanish as their preferred language.
About half of the caregivers reported educational attainment of a Bachelor's degree or higher (52.00%).
Of the patients, approximately half reported using public health insurance (52.00%).
The patients had a mean age of 14.64 and were predominantly female (92.00%).
Most patients had a prior eating disorder-related hospitalization (80.00%), yet few had received non-medical eating disorder treatment (16.00%).

A total of 28 caregivers were identified as eligible by the research team and invited to participate.

After learning about the study, 25 (89.29%) consented to participate, initiated and completed the intervention, completed the Program Feedback Scale, and submitted the pre-and post-intervention survey.
Most of these caregivers (n=18) completed open-ended feedback questions.

Excluding observations more than 1.5 times the interquartile range below the first quartile or above the third quartile, the intervention itself took caregivers about a half hour to complete (M=33.18 minutes; SD=22.13 minutes).

On a 5-point scale, caregivers reported a mean 0.48-point (SD=1.01) increase in their preparedness to help their child manage eating disorder-related distress from pre-to-post intervention (pre-intervention M=3.84, SD=1.25; post-intervention M= 4.32, SD= 0.63).

Regarding preparedness to tolerate their child's distress related to eating disorder treatment, caregivers reported a 0.56-point (SD=0.87) increase from pre-to-post intervention (preintervention M= 3.88, SD=0.88; post-intervention M= 4.44, SD= 0.58), indicating that caregivers went from feeling between neutral and somewhat prepared to feeling between somewhat prepared and very prepared, on average.

When grouped according to selected language, overall mean acceptability was 4.29 (SD=0.53) for the English version and 2.94 (SD=1.15) for the Spanish version.

Of the 25 enrolled caregivers in the study, 18 provided open-ended responses.

Caregivers identified several aspects of Project EMPOWER-ED that supported their understanding of their child's eating disorders and their sense of confidence in their ability to respond to their child's eating disorder behaviors.
Most caregivers described the intervention content as practical and relevant to the challenges their families were experiencing.
Caregivers particularly appreciated the scenarios, examples, and recommended language to use in various challenging situations.
Caregivers noted that these components of the SSI helped translate treatment principles into concrete strategies they could use with their child.
One caregiver stated, "The examples were relatable and helped me better understand the cycle."
Another highlighted the value of receiving "situational advice specific to what we may face."

Caregivers also described learning to recognize their child's eating disorderdriven avoidance behaviors and their own accommodation responses, separating their child from the eating disorder, and strategies to maintain firm eating expectations despite eating disorder-related distress.
One caregiver shared the program "reinforced that parents need to be strong against the eating disorder, not the child."
Another reported that the intervention helped them understand that their child was "not in control" and therefore needed caregiver support in fighting the eating disorder.
2) Validation and Increased Caregiver Confidence.

Several caregivers described that the intervention validated their experience, helped them feel more confident in their ability to support their child's treatment, normalized the difficulty of responding consistently when their child is distressed, and reinforced that maintaining nutrition-related expectations is an important form of caregiver support.
As one caregiver explained, "It was helpful to learn that her fighting back is normal.
That I'm not a bad parent by pushing her to eat."
Another stated that the intervention "helped me find the right words to empathize but stay consistent."

Caregivers also noted the intervention reinforced and validated the strategies they were already implementing, with one noting, "It helped me realize that I was doing some of the right things, and I need to change a few things."
3) Digital and Self-Guided Delivery.
Caregivers generally viewed the digital, self-guided format favorably.
They described the intervention as clear, accessible, and easy to use.
The ability to complete the program independently and at an individualized pace was also valued.
One caregiver stated, "I liked that I could do it at my own pace," while another described the presentation of information as "helpful" and "easy to use."
Some caregivers indicated that the self-guided format was particularly helpful when combined with discussions and support from the treatment team.
As one caregiver noted, "I liked it and combined with live conversations with therapists and psychologists, it's beneficial."
Although feedback was generally favorable, caregivers identified challenges related to the intervention's structure, content, and implementation.
2) Content and Tone.
Two caregivers identified concerns regarding the relevance or tone of the intervention.
One caregiver felt the content was better suited to caregivers of younger children and did not fully reflect the experience of caring for a young adult.
Another described the intervention as "a bit accusatory, which isn't necessarily helpful for parents questioning if they are to blame."
3) Timing and Mode of Delivery.

Timing emerged as a prominent implementation consideration, with most caregivers who commented on timing indicating that Project EMPOWER-ED would have been more helpful earlier in their child's illness course or at the beginning (rather than the end) of the hospital admission, citing alternative times that the intervention would be helpful including at initial diagnosis, before admission, or shortly after admission.
One caregiver recommended providing the intervention at "initial diagnosis because it's not easy or straightforward to identify and combat the behaviors right away."
Another recommended receiving it "earlier, maybe when we first got here" so caregivers would understand that maintaining eating expectations was appropriate and supported by the treatment team.
Of note, these timing preferences were not uniform.
For example, another caregiver valued completing the intervention close to discharge because it reinforced previously learned information.
Others indicated that the program could be useful at multiple points, including both before and after hospitalization.
Some caregivers also expressed a preference for receiving the information directly from a clinician or having an opportunity to discuss the content with a treatment provider.
Caregivers offered several recommendations for future iterations of Project EMPOWER-ED.

Suggestions included dividing the intervention into shorter sections, simplifying survey measures or the wording, and clearly signaling the transition from the intervention to the postintervention assessment.
Caregivers also requested additional scripts for language to use during difficult meals, examples of coping strategies, and practical guidance for navigating challenging meals after discharge.
Several caregivers noted wanting continued access to the intervention content through downloadable notes, emailed resources, or a printed summary of key information.
Additional recommendations included combining the intervention with opportunities for clinician discussion.

This pilot study was an initial investigation into the feasibility and acceptability of a brief web-based caregiver SSI targeting accommodation of eating disorder behaviors during inpatient hospital admission for acute medical stabilization of patients with AN.

Overall, our results suggested that Project EMPOWER-ED had high uptake and completion rates, high overall ratings of acceptability, and promising preliminary changes from pre-to post-intervention on measures of perceived preparedness.
A strong positive result of our pilot study is that feasibility of the SSI was high.

With 89% of possible participants enrolling and completing the intervention, and of those, 72% completing the pre-and post-intervention measures, caregivers seemed to feel that the intervention was manageable and of interest to them.
In addition, time to complete Project EMPOWER-ED was relatively brief with an average completion time of about 33 minutes.
Given the significant burden of caring for a child with an eating disorder, the fact this intervention had such high uptake and was completed efficiently is an important strength.
In particular, embedding this intervention into a hospitalization was shown to be a practical way to provide support to caregivers in need of this information 29 .
text.formatted: In particular, embedding this intervention into a hospitalization was shown to be a practical way to provide support to caregivers in need of this information <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> .

text.text: Taken together, this SSI delivered in this setting may be a highly feasible way to help address the provider shortages, waitlist concerns, and overall lack of evidence-based care in the community facing a particularly highrisk population.
Acceptability pilot data scores were also high.
Qualitative feedback highlighted a number of likely contributors to generally high acceptability, including practical content, feeling validated, and the digital, self-guided format.

It is worth noting, though, that acceptability may have varied between demographic groups, however, the sample size was small overall and there were differences in sample sizes between subgroups, precluding inferential analyses.

Future research should robustly evaluate group differences in the acceptability and effectiveness of Project EMPOWER-ED given that the purpose of the intervention is to address access and equity issues within the eating disorder treatment landscape.
Qualitative data also highlighted some potential barriers to acceptability or areas for improvement.

Despite a relatively short time to completion, some caregivers reported concerns about the length of time to complete the SSI and accompanying measures or the overall burden of completing it during an already overwhelming hospital stay.
It should be noted that some of this feedback was specifically centered on the length of the pre-and post-intervention assessments, as compared to the SSI itself.

Regardless, efforts to continue to work on maximizing brevity in the intervention should be considered, particularly given emerging research on SSIs in other contexts demonstrates that even briefer interventions with reduced text density and duration overall can produce meaningful impacts, raising the possibility that caregivers would find a shorter version of Project EMPOWER-ED helpful. [30] [31] [32] Further, Project EMPOWER-ED was designed to be relevant for caregivers of children through young adults, so future iterations will also ensure that the language, graphics, and vignettes are appropriate across a wider age range and, when possible, offer caregivers a choice of age-relevant scenarios.

text.text: Finally, caregivers gave important feedback on timing.

Many felt that this intervention would have been most helpful at diagnosis or admission to the hospital rather than closer to discharge, which offers actionable guidance for future intervention iterations and trials.

Collectively, these recommendations support retaining the intervention's practical and self-guided components while reducing completion burden, increasing flexibility in timing and delivery of the SSI, and improving the intervention's developmental relevance.
Despite areas for improvement, preliminary data suggests that the intervention could successfully impact important established mechanisms of change for young patients with eating disorders.
Caregivers' assessment of their preparedness to manage their eating disorder-related distress as well as tolerate their child's distress both improved after completing the SSI.

While this cannot be taken to suggest that the intervention is effective due to the small sample size and lack of control group, this is important and promising because these items conceptually align with research suggesting that distress tolerance reduces accommodation which can exacerbate harmful eating disorder behaviors 10 .

text.text: In addition, the identified changes in caregiver preparedness are consistent with findings from the original anxiety-focused SSI on which Project EMPOWER-ED was based 20, 21 .

text.text: This preliminary data is a promising step in the right direction toward improving caregivers' abilities in supporting their children's eating disorder recovery.
This study has several important strengths that merit discussion.
First, its mixed-methods design allows for rich feedback alongside quantitative data, allowing caregiver perspectives to contextualize the numeric findings.
In addition, this study achieved a high completion rate, despite recruiting from a clinically burdened inpatient population.
This offers an important perspective on how we can support a very acute and high-risk population during a particularly sensitive time.

Finally, the collaboration amongst a multidisciplinary group of creators that included both the original intervention developers as well as pediatric psychologists with expertise in eating disorders strengthened both the SSI's clinical relevance and fidelity to evidence-based principles.
Despite these strengths, this study also has limitations.
Most importantly, this was a small pilot study without a control or randomization, limiting our ability to draw inferences about clinical effectiveness.
This was a narrow sample in that it was limited to a single site and specific to caregivers of youth with anorexia in one hospital.
We currently lack data about whether this SSI might help a broader population of caregivers, possibly at different stages of care.
Given caregiver feedback on timing, it would be particularly beneficial to explore for whom and when during treatment it would be most helpful to offer this intervention 33 .
text.formatted: Given caregiver feedback on timing, it would be particularly beneficial to explore for whom and when during treatment it would be most helpful to offer this intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> .

text.text: Additionally, while our multidisciplinary team of developers brought strong clinical expertise, it did not include community stakeholders or individuals with lived experience.

Key next steps for Project EMPOWER-ED include larger, multi-site trials with more diverse samples, more rigorous efficacy testing with stronger experimental controls, incorporation of community stakeholder input into intervention refinement, and evaluation of the SSI's impact across different stages of the recovery journey.

Taken together, these findings suggest that a brief, web-based SSI can be feasibly and acceptably delivered to caregivers during a uniquely stressful window of their child's medical hospitalization for anorexia nervosa.

Preliminary improvements in caregiver ability to manage and tolerate distress, alongside caregivers' own reports of increased confidence and validation, offer an encouraging early signal that this low-cost, scalable approach may help address a persistent gap in caregiver support during eating disorder treatment.

A multi-site trial, informed by community stakeholder input and designed to test timing and setting directly, represents the next step toward determining not just whether Project EMPOWER-ED works, but for whom and when it can be most useful.

Four caregivers described the intervention and/or accompanying assessment measures as too lengthy.
One caregiver described the program as containing "helpful information" but noted that "it was long and felt overwhelming and too much at one time."
Another stated that it was "a little too long with all the questions at the start but helpful overall."
Caregivers also identified instances of confusing wording, including double negatives in standardized measures and unclear transitions.

One caregiver recommended adding language explaining that participants would be asked similar questions before the program and then again after completing it, noting, "I thought it took me back to the start [of the program]."
Other challenges included the cognitive demand of generating written responses to scenarios and uncertainty about whether intervention resources could be accessed again later.
No follow-up data reported: Although we originally planned to report 1-week and 3month follow-up data, we did not report these data because the sample size was already small and attrition was high.
Specifically, only16 participants completed the 1-week follow-up and only 10 participants completed the 3-month follow-up.
